meta.title: Orchard — a garden weather station
meta.subtitle: Round 2 of 3
meta.headline: Two things left to draw a line around.
meta.lede: Last round settled it: a **frost warning** for you alone, handed over as a build plan. This round draws the edges — how much of the orchard it covers, and how you will know it worked.
meta.closingAsk: Update the scope from these answers, then tell me what is still open.

scope.label: What we're trying to achieve
scope.text: Warn you when it is freezing in the orchard, on your phone, in time to do something about it.

scope.label: What we hand over
scope.text: A build plan you follow yourself: ordered steps, a parts list, and a test for the first cold night.

scope.label: What's in and what's out
scope.text: One station was assumed last round. Now that frost is the goal, the low corner may need its own reading.
scope.reopened: Frost pools at the bottom of the slope, so one mast may not answer the question we just agreed on.

scope.label: How we know it's done
scope.text: Surviving one cold night was assumed. A warning that fires and one that is right are not the same thing.
scope.reopened: You changed the warning to a live reading, which changes entirely what a correct warning looks like.

scope.label: Fixed facts we work inside
scope.text: Mains power in the shed, twelve metres from the mast. No cloud account. You are the only person alerted.

context.title: Where this stands
context.note: The goal is fixed and narrow: a live freezing warning, to your phone. Everything below is about how far it reaches and how you check it.

items.desc: cold air pooling at the low end of a slope
a warning that fired on a night nothing froze

questions.context: Cold air runs downhill and pools at the bottom of your slope. The mast is at the top, which is the warmest corner of the orchard.
breakdown: One reading at the top: cheapest, but it will miss the cold nights.
A second reading at the bottom: more to mount, and it tells the truth.
questions.question: Should the low corner get its own reading?
questions.why: The mast sits in the warmest spot, so a station up there would quietly under-report exactly the nights you built it for.
questions.switchIf: Stay with one reading if you would rather get something working and add the second next winter.

options.label: One reading at the mast
options.detail: Simplest, but blind to the frost pocket.

options.label: Add one at the low corner
options.detail: Two readings; warn on whichever is colder.

options.label: A reading every fifty metres
options.detail: A real sensor network, and a real project.

questions.context: Keeping every reading forever is easy to say and slow to regret. What you keep decides how much of this is storage work.
breakdown: This season only: nothing to manage, and no history to look back on.
Keep everything: you can compare years, and you own a growing pile of files.
questions.example: One file per day at a reading a minute is about fifty kilobytes — a decade of that still fits on the smallest memory card you can buy.
questions.question: How far back should the record go?
questions.why: Storage is free at this size and comparing two springs is the first thing you will want, so keeping it all costs nothing real.
questions.switchIf: Keep only this season if you would rather never think about backups or old files at all.

options.label: This season only
options.detail: Wipe and start again each spring.

options.label: Keep everything
options.detail: One CSV file per day, kept indefinitely.

options.label: Keep a daily summary
options.detail: Minimum and maximum only; the detail is dropped.

questions.context: You changed the warning to fire on a live reading. That makes it simple to build and it makes being wrong much easier to spot.
breakdown: Against your own eyes: you check the grass in the morning.
Against a second thermometer: slower to set up, and it settles arguments.
questions.example: A cheap glass minimum thermometer left in the orchard overnight records the coldest point, which you read the next morning.
questions.question: What do we check the warning against?
questions.why: A second thermometer costs a few pounds and turns a hunch about the sensor into something you can actually show.
questions.switchIf: Go with your own eyes if you would rather not buy anything and are happy judging it by the frost on the grass.

options.label: Frost on the grass
options.detail: Free, immediate, and hard to argue with.

options.label: A minimum thermometer
options.detail: Read each morning; settles the argument.

options.label: The nearest weather station
options.detail: Miles away and on different ground.

questions.context: You raised this yourself in the notes. A station that has quietly stopped sending looks exactly like a station reporting no frost.
breakdown: Say nothing: silence is indistinguishable from a mild night.
Warn on silence: one more alert, and you find out before the frost does.
questions.question: What should happen when a sensor goes quiet?
questions.why: Silent failure is the one way this station lets you down without ever looking broken, and a nightly check costs almost nothing.
questions.switchIf: Leave it silent if you would rather check the shed display yourself than get another notification.

options.label: Warn me the same evening
options.detail: One message if nothing arrived in an hour.

options.label: Show it on the display only
options.detail: Visible if you look; silent if you do not.

options.label: Do nothing
options.detail: You find out on the morning it mattered.
